definition: An official royal messenger sent to represent one ruler at another king’s court—such as Benin’s envoy to Lisbon in Portugal.
A sacred raised clay platform inside the Benin palace holding cast brass heads, carved ivory tusks, and bells to honour past Obas.
Famous royal plaques, heads, and figures made in Benin City—mostly cast from golden brass alongside bronze and carved ivory.
A bright golden metal alloy mixing copper and zinc, melted in clay pots by Igun Street casters to create royal Benin plaques.
Polished red sea-coral beads woven into heavy crowns, high collars, and tunics worn as sacred symbols of the Oba’s rank.
Small glossy white ocean shells used across West African markets as everyday small-change money for buying food and cloth.
A thick, heat-proof clay melting pot placed in a roaring charcoal furnace to turn solid brass manillas into glowing liquid.
A line of kings or queens from the same royal family—such as Benin’s unbroken dynasty of Obas founded by Oba Eweka I around AD 1180.
A wide, leaf-shaped ceremonial iron sword spun high in the air by Benin chiefs while dancing to honour the sacred Oba.
The people, language, and royal capital (Benin City) of the historic Kingdom of Benin in modern southern Nigeria.
An organised royal group of specialist craftworkers—such as brass-casters, ivory-carvers, or weavers—living in their own city street.
Benin’s busy river harbour (also called Ughoton) where European ships anchored from 1485 to seek the Oba’s permission to trade.
Sacred Yoruba city north-west of Benin, famed for lifelike brass heads and Prince Oranmiyan, father of Benin’s first Oba Eweka I.
Benin’s joyful annual royal thanksgiving ceremony giving thanks to ancestors and renewing the sacred strength of the Oba.
The historic royal street in Benin City where hereditary families of the brass-casters’ guild have poured molten brass for centuries.
Smooth creamy-white elephant tusk carved by royal Benin sculptors into Queen Mother masks, altar tusks, and saltcellars.
Deep ditches and steep red-earth banks dug by hand across 16,000 kilometres of rainforest around Benin City and Edo villages.
Royal Edo title meaning Queen Mother, created around 1515 by Oba Esigie to honour his wise mother Idia with her own palace.
Rich iron-red tropical clay soil in southern Nigeria that dries rock-hard in the sun to form Benin’s walls and polished houses.
Sculpting a detailed beeswax figure, coating it in clay, melting the wax out, and pouring liquid brass into the hollow mould.
Heavy horseshoe-shaped brass and copper bracelets brought by European ships to trade for Benin pepper, cloth, and ivory.
A West African river fish able to breathe on damp mud—carved on Benin plaques to link the Oba with sea-god Olokun.
The sacred king of Benin, honoured as "Leopard of the House" and living link between Edo people and royal ancestors.
Early rulers of Benin (c. AD 900–1180) before the Oba dynasty, whose royal title meant "Kings of the Sky".
Important Edo god of great waters, rivers, wealth, and fertility, honoured alongside supreme creator god Osanobua.
Rich red oil pressed from West African oil-palm fruit—used in Edo cooking, street lamps, and 19th-century global trade.
The February 1897 British military invasion that burned Benin’s royal palace, exiled Oba Ovonramwen, and looted over 4,000 artworks.
Rightfully returning looted cultural treasures—such as 1897 Benin Bronzes—from foreign museums back to their home country.
